analysis.one_liner: Bars company executives and directors from trading stock in the window before major corporate news is publicly filed.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When something big happens at a public company—a merger, the loss of a major customer, an executive departure—the company must disclose it on a Form 8-K filing, usually within days. In that window, executives and directors already know the news and can legally buy or sell stock before outside investors can react. This bill would direct the SEC to write rules requiring companies to adopt policies prohibiting those trades, and would block executives from dodging the ban with trading plans adopted after they learn the news. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors who trade on public information rather than private knowledge. Closing the gap between when a major corporate event happens and when the company files its 8-K disclosure means insiders cannot sell a crashing stock or buy a rising one before regular investors even know the news exists. Retirement savers benefit indirectly, since mutual fund managers invested in these companies face the same information asymmetry.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary stock investors and retirement savers

how_it_helps.text: Directs the SEC to issue rules requiring public companies to establish policies that prohibit executive officers and directors from buying or selling their company's stock between the moment a significant corporate event occurs and the moment the company files the required Form 8-K public disclosure of it [S3].

Closes a loophole in Rule 10b5-1 trading plans: the SEC may not exempt a trading plan adopted by an executive or director after they learned of the triggering event but before the company disclosed it, so insiders cannot pre-plan trades with foreknowledge of undisclosed news [S3].

Pre-announced events are treated fairly: if the company already made the news public through a Regulation FD-compliant press release, the trading ban does not apply, since outside investors then have the same information insiders do [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporate executives, directors, and major shareholders who trade during the disclosure window. The bill only restricts trades made with information the public does not yet have, so it costs insiders a source of trading profit but does not affect any transaction an outside investor could have made on the same information. Public companies face a modest compliance cost to write and maintain the required policies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate insiders who trade on undisclosed news

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves substantial discretion to the SEC to exempt automatic trades, advance-election trades, and Rule 10b5-1 plan trades meeting existing conditions, so its real-world strength would depend heavily on rules the agency has not yet written [S3].
Compliance burden: every reporting company must establish and maintain new trading policies, controls, and procedures, a cost that falls on companies of all sizes [S3].

Some exemptions are built in: investment companies and their advisers, which already must maintain codes of ethics under existing regulation, are carved out entirely, and the bill applies only to trades between the event and the 8-K filing, not to the broader range of inside information executives hold [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted and real: the gap between a corporate event and its 8-K filing is exactly when insider trading is easiest to disguise, because the trade is legal under current law even though the trader knows material nonpublic news. The costs are modest—paperwork for companies and foregone trading profits for insiders with no legitimate basis to trade. The bill is narrow; it does not create new private lawsuits or penalties beyond what the SEC writes into its rules, and some critics would say a well-drafted insider trading enforcement regime already covers the worst cases. But the one-year trading window it targets is a recognized blind spot, and the bill's fix is proportionate to the problem.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Carolyn Maloney introduced the 8-K Trading Gap Act on July 16, 2021 [S1, S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day and received no further action—no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote [S5].
Not a single representative cosponsored the bill [S4].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate executives and directors keep their ability to trade on major corporate news during the days or weeks before the company must file its 8-K disclosure. Companies avoid writing new trading policies, and the SEC is not directed to close the trading-plan loophole. Ordinary investors remain exposed to trades made with information they do not have.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate insiders who trade before disclosures

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, letting it die in committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split on its merits was ever recorded; it had one Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of any party.

industries.industry: Corporate executives and directors of public companies
industries.note: The bill's direct target: it would prohibit insiders from buying or selling company stock between the moment a major event occurs and the moment it is publicly filed, closing a window in which such trades are currently legal. Insiders would give up trading profits available only through information the public does not yet have.

Each reporting company would have to establish and maintain trading policies, controls, and procedures. That is a real cost, but it is administrative; the substance of the bill restricts individual insiders rather than company operations.
These firms are exempted because they already operate under required codes of ethics. They gain a cleaner market without new obligations of their own.
